summary: A proposal by Jon Postel that willing hosts run a Discard process for debugging and measurement. It listens for a connection, completes the Initial Connection Protocol, and throws away every piece of data it receives right away. The connection ends when it is closed.

plainLanguage.summary: Like a mailbox that eats every letter you put in. Nothing comes back, but you can see how fast you can send things, which helps test the network.

questions: how does the discard process work
subtitle: Hosts are invited to run a process that throws away all data it receives, for debugging and measurement.

tldr.problem: Hosts needed a simple service to help with debugging and measurement of the network.
tldr.mechanism: A willing Host runs a Discard process that waits for a connection, performs the Initial Connection Protocol (ICP), then discards all data it receives.
tldr.outcome: The proposal is voluntary: it applies to those hosts which are willing to implement it.

sections.title: The Discard Process Proposal
sections.content: Jon Postel suggests that, for debugging and measurement purposes, those hosts which are willing implement a Discard process. Participation is optional.
sections.plainLanguage: Some computers are asked to offer a simple test service, if they want to.

sections.title: How the Discard Process Works
sections.content:
The process listens for a request for connection and executes the Initial Connection Protocol (ICP) as specified in NIC 7104, the "Current Network Protocols" notebook. After ICP completes, it waits for data from the network.

When data arrives it is discarded at once and the buffer space is re-allocated. The process ends when the network connections are closed.
sections.plainLanguage: The computer waits for someone to knock, says hello the standard way, then throws away whatever it gets.

sections.title: Status
sections.content: It is a short suggestion from Jon Postel at UCLA and sets no other requirements: any Host that is willing may implement the process, and no Host is required to.
sections.plainLanguage: It is just a friendly suggestion, not a rule.
